title: Charles House
author: Austin Maynard Architects
quality: Medium · project documentation. Resident outcomes have not been verified.
evidence: Shared home / future grandparent suite. Kew, Melbourne, Australia; 2017; One adaptable family house.
interpretation: Use XL as a home with two credible daily routines, rather than a large apartment with an extra bedroom.
question: Can two generations each keep their own daily routine in the XL dwelling?
implication: Draw XL in three states: young family; grandparent co-residence; adult-child independence.

title: Mahogany House
author: R ARCHITECTURE
quality: Medium · project documentation. Resident outcomes have not been verified.
evidence: Related households with a shared centre. Mount Waverley, Melbourne, Australia; 2023; One house / two domestic pods.
interpretation: A shared threshold can connect two homes while their living rooms remain distinct.
question: Can either household pass the shared threshold and withdraw to its own living room?
implication: Compare direct-facing and offset living-room windows around an S–M shared front yard.

title: 3 Generation House
author: BETA office for architecture and the city
quality: Medium · project documentation. Resident outcomes have not been verified.
evidence: Independent family homes with future reallocation. Buiksloterham, Amsterdam, Netherlands; 2018; Two stacked apartments / 450 m².
interpretation: This is the closest match to the S-above-L rule: vertical proximity needs an independent accessible route.
question: Can a grandparent visit family one floor below by lift and return through their own front door?
implication: Draw S-above-L with the lift route, optional family link and a closed-link state.

title: Veil + Co. House
author: Kirsten Johnstone Architecture
mix: Main home + secondary dwelling on one lot
quality: Medium · project documentation. Resident outcomes have not been verified.
evidence: Detached family accommodation along a covered route. Currimundi, Sunshine Coast, Australia; Built; documented in 2025 award; Main home + secondary dwelling on one lot.
interpretation: Translate the covered street into a sheltered gallery with distinct front doors and places to pause.
question: Can someone stop at an entry without blocking the sheltered route?
implication: Draw a gallery-to-front-yard section in open and screened states, including rain cover and a clear bypass.

title: La Borda
author: Lacol
quality: Medium · project documentation. Resident outcomes have not been verified.
evidence: Mixed-household community / shared domestic facilities. Barcelona, Spain; 2018; 28 cooperative homes.
interpretation: Make shared laundry a useful, accessible destination; do not require a resident to socialise to perform a necessary task.
question: Can a resident collect washing without joining a gathering?
implication: Locate laundry on an everyday route with a quiet bypass, seating and a management note.

title: Marmalade Lane
author: Mole Architects; TOWN / Trivselhus
quality: Medium · project documentation. Resident outcomes have not been verified.
evidence: Intergenerational cohousing neighbourhood. Cambridge, United Kingdom; 2018; 42 houses and apartments.
interpretation: Give the cluster a recognisable shared address, but retain each home's own door and outdoor retreat.
question: Where can a household sit outside while choosing how much contact to have?
implication: Test the same four-home cluster with related families and unrelated households.

title: Giesserei
author: Galli Rudolf Architekten; Gesewo
quality: Medium · project documentation. Resident outcomes have not been verified.
evidence: Mixed-generation cooperative with varied dwelling types. Winterthur, Switzerland; 2013; 155 apartments / six-storey courtyard block.
interpretation: A large building can contain several small neighbourhoods. Group S/M/L around a legible landing rather than one anonymous corridor.
question: How many front doors share a landing, and who can see into them?
implication: Compare a cluster landing and long gallery for homes served, route length and sightlines.

title: Generationernes Hus
author: RUM and ERIK Arkitekter; Sweco engineering
quality: Medium · project documentation. Resident outcomes have not been verified.
evidence: Mixed-generation housing with staffed care. Aarhus, Denmark; 2020; 304 homes plus care and childcare.
interpretation: Distinguish informal neighbourly help from professional care. Your family cluster can support proximity without becoming an aged-care facility.
question: Do visitors and care workers reach the intended home directly?
implication: Map voluntary family contact separately from deliveries, visitors and any future care visit.

title: Hunziker Areal / mehr als wohnen
author: Futurafrosch + Duplex masterplan; five architecture teams
quality: Medium · project documentation. Resident outcomes have not been verified.
evidence: Mixed-age cooperative neighbourhood. Zurich, Switzerland; 2014–2015; 13 buildings / approximately 1,200 residents.
interpretation: Offer several degrees of connection: independent home, family cluster, shared building and public street.
question: Who can enter each shared space, and who looks after it?
implication: Assign each shared space a user group, catchment and responsible manager; remove redundant facilities.

title: Strandeiland M3
author: BETA with LEVS, MEESVISSER and DELVA; client AM
quality: Medium · project documentation. Resident outcomes have not been verified.
evidence: Planned intergenerational block / managed age mix. Amsterdam, Netherlands; Definitive design; programme 2023–2027; Part of a 344-home collaborative development.
interpretation: The spatial cluster also needs an occupancy strategy if adjacent S and M homes are intended for related households.
question: How could related households secure adjacent dwellings over time?
implication: Test allocation, turnover and unrelated occupancy without changing the architectural shell.

title: One roof, three generations
author: Jacinta Cleary · Sanctuary, 2025
access: Common entry and courtyard lead to individual front doors.
shared: Backyard and pool serve both households.
quality: Project profile with architect interview. Documents the arrangement, with limited evidence on daily use.
evidence: One courtyard serves two independent homes, each with its own entrance.
interpretation: A shared arrival space could make short visits possible while preserving a clear invitation threshold.
implication: Draw the S/M pair at 1:100. Trace returning home, visiting family and passing a closed front door.
question: Can either household reach its door without looking into the other living room?

title: Apartment Design Guide
author: NSW Government · Part 4, §4K
mix: Studios to family apartments in the illustrated section.
access: Figure 4K.4 uses split-level apartments to reduce common circulation.
shared: Larger units can occupy levels with greater outdoor space.
quality: Government design guidance. Transfer to Adelaide requires local testing.
evidence: Section 4K recommends varied unit sizes and flexible configurations across life stages.
interpretation: A section through S, L and XL may reveal opportunities missed in a typical floor plan.
implication: Draw an S above an L alongside a two-storey XL. Mark every entry and step-free route.
question: Which household relationships remain practical when a resident cannot use stairs?

title: Terracotta House
author: Austin Maynard Architects · Project account
mix: Two independent houses with a shared pavilion
access: The shared building sits between the homes.
shared: Central pavilion combines laundry, guest accommodation and social uses.
quality: Architect account establishes program and arrangement. Actual use frequency is unmeasured.
evidence: Two households share a garden and a third building containing everyday amenities.
interpretation: A shared destination between dwellings could support visits without opening either home.
implication: Place the laundry and a seat on the courtyard route. Draw a direct bypass for residents heading home.
question: Who controls access when the shared room is used by a guest?

title: Changing perceptions of family
author: Easthope, Liu, Burnley & Judd · Journal of Sociology
quality: Peer-reviewed empirical study. Survey of 392 people, 21 diaries and 21 follow-up interviews. The sample concerns co-residence.
evidence: The study examines how residents understand family through the experience of cohabitation.
interpretation: Related households living across a landing may share some routines while negotiating different boundaries.
implication: Use two household timetables to test the S/M entry arrangement during visits, departures and periods of retreat.
question: Which observations about co-residence transfer to relatives in separate dwellings?

title: Nightingale Marrickville
author: SJB · Nightingale Housing
access: Entry geometry needs a plan check.
shared: Shared laundries, garden terrace, dining and living spaces.
quality: Provider account documents amenities and unit count. Resident outcomes require separate evidence.
evidence: Small dwellings are paired with several shared domestic facilities.
interpretation: Clustering everyday tasks near a shared route may give residents a reason to linger.
implication: Overlay laundry trips and direct lift-to-door routes on the external walkway plan.
question: Can someone collect washing and return home without crossing a group activity?

title: Multi-generation households in Australian cities
author: Liu & Easthope · AHURI Final Report 181
access: Census records do not describe entrance arrangements.
shared: Household data do not map shared-space use.
quality: Longitudinal census analysis, 1981–2006. Historical categories constrain comparison with neighbouring households.
evidence: The report tracks changing household composition using multiple Australian censuses.
interpretation: Separate dwellings occupied by relatives can fall outside a co-residence measure.
implication: Record dwelling count and family relationship separately in the Southwark occupancy diagrams.
question: What local evidence would support the proposed share of S dwellings?

title: Intergenerational Cottage
author: main frank · Project account
mix: Extended cottage accommodating changing family configurations
access: Separate entries allow households to arrive independently.
shared: Communal garden and private deck offer different degrees of contact.
quality: Designer account describes changes in household use. No independent occupancy study is cited.
evidence: The project accommodates family changes through separate entries and a combination of shared and private outdoor space.
interpretation: A private outdoor retreat may remain important even where relatives share a garden.
implication: Furnish the XL dwelling for two stages of family life. Preserve access to a private outdoor seat in both.
question: Which room can change use without moving plumbing or blocking circulation?
